title: Collecting and Organising Data: Tallies, Frequency Tables and the Mode
seo_title: Grade 5 Collecting and Organising Data Worksheets with Answers (CAPS Maths)
standard_text: Collect data on everyday things using tally marks and tables for recording; order data from smallest group to largest group; summarise and interpret data using the mode.
meta_desc: Free CAPS Grade 5 data handling worksheets: tally marks, frequency tables, comparing data and the mode. 100 questions with memos.
key_big: The mode is the most common value.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • Collect data by asking a question and recording each answer with tally marks.
  • A tally group of 5 is 4 lines crossed by a fifth line.
  • A frequency table shows how many times each answer appears.
  • The mode is the answer that appears most often.

Examples

Example

Shoe sizes: 4, 5, 5, 6, 5, 4, 7

5 appears 3 times

Answer: the mode is 5

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
A group of 4A tally group is 5.
The biggest numberThe mode is the most common.
The wrong rowUse a ruler to follow the row.

faq.q: What does CAPS Grade 5 say about collecting data?
faq.a: Collect data using tally marks and tables, order data, and summarise data using the mode.
Yes, if two values appear equally most often.
It is easier to read and compare.

items.q: How many silver cars were there?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. The Silver row has 2 groups of 5 and 4 more: 2 × 5 = 10, and 10 + 4 = 14.

items.q: How many red cars were there?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. The Red row has 4 groups of 5 and 1 more: 4 × 5 = 20, and 20 + 1 = 21.

items.q: How many sparrows were seen?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. The Sparrow row has 3 groups of 5 and 2 more: 3 × 5 = 15, and 15 + 2 = 17.

items.q: Which row shows 16 birds?
items.e: 16 = 5 + 5 + 5 + 1. Look for 3 groups of 5 and 1 single mark. That is the Blackbird row.
Count each row: Soccer 16, Netball 22, Swimming 20, Cricket 24. Then add: 16 + 22 + 20 + 24 = 82 learners.

items.q: How many buses went past the school?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. The Bus row has 4 groups of 5 and 2 more: 4 × 5 = 20, and 20 + 2 = 22.

items.q: What is the difference between the biggest and the smallest number of vehicles?
items.e: The biggest is Bus (22). The smallest is Lorry (8). Difference means subtract: 22 − 8 = 14.

items.q: Which row shows 7 votes?
items.e: 7 = 5 + 2. Look for 1 group of 5 and 2 single marks. That is the Apple row.

items.q: How many votes are shown in the tally chart altogether?
items.e: Count each row: Apple 7, Banana 24, Grapes 12, Pear 9. Then add: 7 + 24 + 12 + 9 = 52 votes.

items.q: How many books did Grade 3 borrow on Monday?
items.e: Find the Monday row, then go across to the Grade 3 column. The cell says 16.

items.q: How many books were borrowed on Thursday altogether?
items.e: Add the two cells in the Thursday row: 8 + 28 = 36.

items.q: On which day were the most books borrowed altogether?
items.e: Add each row: Mon 50, Tue 30, Wed 43, Thu 36. The biggest total is 50 on Monday.

items.q: How many books did Grade 4 borrow on Wednesday?
items.e: Find the Wednesday row, then go across to the Grade 4 column. The cell says 31.

items.q: How many books did Grade 3 borrow from Monday to Thursday?
items.e: Add the whole Grade 3 column: 9 + 27 + 8 + 21 = 65.

items.q: How many books did Grade 3 borrow on Monday?
items.e: Find the Monday row, then go across to the Grade 3 column. The cell says 21.

items.q: How many books were borrowed on Tuesday altogether?
items.e: Add the two cells in the Tuesday row: 27 + 17 = 44.

items.q: How many books did Grade 4 borrow from Monday to Thursday?
items.e: Add the whole Grade 4 column: 32 + 17 + 9 + 10 = 68.

items.q: How many silver cars were there?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. The Silver row has 2 groups of 5 and 4 more: 2 × 5 = 10, and 10 + 4 = 14.

items.q: How many black cars were there?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. The Black row has 1 group of 5 and 1 more: 1 × 5 = 5, and 5 + 1 = 6.

items.q: How many learners chose soccer?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. The Soccer row has 2 groups of 5 and 4 more: 2 × 5 = 10, and 10 + 4 = 14.

items.q: How many learners in 5B have a packed lunch?
items.e: Find the Packed lunch row, then go across to the 5B column: 9. (11 is 5A.)

items.q: How many learners in 5A have a school dinner?
items.e: School dinner row, 5A column: 14.

items.q: How many learners are in 5A?
items.e: The Total row at the bottom gives each class. 5A: 14 + 11 + 3 = 28.

items.q: How many more learners have a school dinner than a packed lunch?
items.e: Use the Total column. School dinner: 31. Packed lunch: 20. 31 − 20 = 11. (Using only one class gives 3 or 8.)

items.q: How many learners are in Grade 5 altogether?
items.e: The bottom right cell is the total of everything: 28 + 30 = 58 learners.

items.q: What time does the swimming pool close on Saturday?
items.e: Find the Saturday row, then go across to the Closes column: 17:30 (5:30 pm).

items.q: How long is the pool open on Sunday?
items.e: 09:30 to 15:30 is 6 hours. 15:30 to 16:00 is 30 minutes. So the pool is open 6 hours 30 minutes. (1 600 − 930 = 670 treats an hour as 100 minutes.)

items.q: On which day is the pool open for the longest time?
items.e: Work out each day: Monday 13 hours 30 minutes, Wednesday 15 hours, Saturday 9 hours 30 minutes, Sunday 6 hours 30 minutes. Wednesday is the longest. (Monday opens just as early, but closes earlier.)

items.q: How many adult tickets were sold on Friday?
items.e: The adult row adds up to 183. Thursday is 86. 183 − 86 = 97 tickets. Check: 86 + 97 = 183.

items.q: How many child tickets were sold altogether?
items.e: Add along the Child row: 124 + 158 = 282. Remember to exchange: 4 + 8 = 12 ones.

items.q: What number is missing from the table?
items.e: The bottom right cell is the total of all tickets. Add the Total column: 183 + 282 = 465. Check with the Total row: 210 + 255 = 465.

items.q: On which day were more child tickets sold, and how many more?
items.e: Child row: Thursday 124, Friday 158. Friday is more: 158 − 124 = 34.

items.q: How many boys cannot swim 25 m?
items.e: There are 45 boys. 38 of them can swim. 45 − 38 = 7 boys cannot.

items.q: How many learners are in Grade 5 altogether?
items.e: Add the Total column: 45 + 47 = 92. 5 + 7 = 12 ones, so exchange 10 ones for 1 ten. Check with the Total row: 79 + 13 = 92.

items.q: How many learners come to school by bus?
items.e: Add the numbers you know: 23 + 14 + 8 + 5 = 50. The total is 60, so 60 − 50 = 10 learners come by bus.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups in 5s, then count on the single marks: 3 groups of 5 and 3 more: 3 × 5 = 15, and 15 + 3 = 18.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups in 5s, then count on the single marks: 5 groups of 5 and 2 more: 5 × 5 = 25, and 25 + 2 = 27.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups in 5s, then count on the single marks: 6 groups of 5 and 4 more: 6 × 5 = 30, and 30 + 4 = 34.
Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups in 5s, then count on the single marks: 8 groups of 5 and 1 more: 8 × 5 = 40, and 40 + 1 = 41.
23 = 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 3, so look for 4 groups of 5 and 3 single marks. That is C. A shows 28 (one group of 5 too many); B shows 22 (one single mark is missing); D shows 24 (one single mark too many).

items.q: Ofentse will draw a pictograph of these votes: 40, 25, 35 and 50. She wants whole symbols only, and as few symbols as she can. Which key should she use?
items.e: Every number is in the 5 times table, so a key of 5 gives whole symbols: 8, 5, 7 and 10. A key of 10 or 2 would need half symbols for 25 and 35. A key of 1 needs 150 symbols.

items.q: Pieter will draw a pictograph of 60, 90, 40 and 70 learners. He wants whole symbols only, and as few symbols as he can. Which key should he use?
items.e: Every number is a multiple of 10, so a key of 10 gives whole symbols: 6, 9, 4 and 7 (26 symbols). A key of 5 also works, but it needs twice as many symbols (52).

items.q: Ethan will draw a bar graph of 12, 18, 6 and 14 votes. Every column must end exactly on a gridline, and he wants no more than 10 gridlines above 0. What should the scale go up in?
items.e: Counting in 1s needs 18 gridlines, which is too many. Counting in 2s needs 9 gridlines (2 to 18), and every number is even, so every column ends on a line. In 5s or 10s, 12, 18, 6 and 14 would end between lines.

items.q: Thandi will draw a bar graph of 35, 50, 20 and 45 tickets. Every column must end exactly on a gridline, and she wants no more than 10 gridlines above 0. What should the scale go up in?
items.e: Counting in 5s needs 10 gridlines (5 to 50), and every number is in the 5 times table. 1s or 2s need far too many lines (50 or 25). In 10s, 35 and 45 would end halfway between lines.

items.q: Raffle tickets sold (frequency table): 4A 45, 4B 70, 4C 30, 4D 55. Which bar graph shows the same data?
items.e: C matches every number (the scale goes up in 10s). A: two columns are the wrong way round; B: a column is on the line below (it should be halfway between two lines); D: one column is one line too high.

items.q: Ice blocks sold (frequency table): Mon 20, Tue 30, Wed 15, Thu 25. Which pictograph shows the same data?
items.e: A matches every number (each symbol = 5). B: two rows are the wrong way round; C: one row has a symbol too many; D: one row is missing a symbol.
D matches every number (each symbol = 10). A: two rows are the wrong way round; B: a half symbol is drawn as a whole symbol; C: one row has a symbol too many.

items.q: The pictograph and the bar graph show the same data. How many tickets should the missing 4C column show?
items.e: Read the 4C row of the pictograph. Each circle = 10 tickets. The 4C row has 3 circles and half a circle: 3 × 10 = 30, and half of 10 is 5, so 30 + 5 = 35 tickets. Draw the 4C column up to 35.
Read the Thandi row of the pictograph. Each star = 2 books. The Thandi row has 4 stars and half a star: 4 × 2 = 8, and half of 2 is 1, so 8 + 1 = 9 books. Draw the Thandi column up to 9.

items.q: How many learners read 3 books?
items.e: Each dot is one learner. Count the dots above 3: there are 5. (3 is the number of books, not the number of learners.)

items.q: How many learners are shown on the dot plot?
items.e: Each dot is one learner, so count every dot: 2 + 4 + 6 + 5 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 23. (7 counts the stacks, and 28 adds the numbers on the line.)

items.q: What is the most common number of books read?
items.e: The tallest stack of dots is above 2 (6 dots). So 2 books is the most common answer. 6 is how many learners, not how many books.

items.q: How many learners read more than 4 books?
items.e: More than 4 means 5, 6 or 7 books. There are 2 dots above 5, none above 6 and 1 above 7: 2 + 1 = 3. (6 also counts the learners who read exactly 4.)

items.q: Which statement is true?
c: More learners read 1 book than 5 books.
The same number of learners read 2 books and 3 books.
Every learner read at least 1 book.
items.e: 1 book has 4 dots and 5 books has 2 dots, so this is true. Only 1 learner read 7 books. 2 learners read 0 books. 2 books has 6 dots and 3 books has 5.

items.q: How many learners have no brothers or sisters?
items.e: No brothers or sisters means the answer 0. There are 4 dots above 0.

items.q: How many learners have 2 or more brothers and sisters?
items.e: 2 or more means 2, 3, 4 or 5: 6 + 3 + 0 + 2 = 11. (5 leaves out the learners with exactly 2.)

items.q: How many more learners have 1 brother or sister than have 3?
items.e: Above 1 there are 9 dots. Above 3 there are 3 dots. 9 − 3 = 6. (2 is 3 − 1, the numbers on the line, not the dots.)

items.q: Palesa asked 4A, “How many brothers and sisters do you have?” She wants to show each answer as one dot above a number line. Which display should she use?
items.e: A dot plot has a number line, and each answer is one dot above its number. It suits numerical data such as 0, 1, 2 or 3 brothers and sisters.

items.q: Ethan says Graph B shows fewer cans than Graph A because its columns are shorter. Is he right?
c: Yes. The columns in Graph B are shorter.
No. Graph B shows more cans.
Yes. Graph B has fewer gridlines.
No. Both graphs show the same numbers.
items.e: Graph A goes up in 5s and Graph B goes up in 10s. Read both: 4A 20, 4B 35, 4C 40, 4D 25. The numbers are the same; only the scale is different. Always read the scale, not the height.

items.q: Read Graph B. How many cans did 4B collect?
items.e: Graph B goes up in 10s. The 4B column ends halfway between 30 and 40, so it shows 35. (3 counts the grid spaces. Graph A shows 35 too.)

items.q: Each dot is one learner. What is the mode of the data?
items.e: The mode is the value that appears most often: the tallest stack of dots. 9 learners have 1 pet, so the mode is 1 pet. (9 is how many learners, and 6 is the highest value, not the mode.)

items.q: How many learners have 2 pets?
items.e: Count the dots above 2: there are 6. Each dot is one learner.

items.q: How many learners are in 5C?
items.e: Each dot is one learner, so count all the dots: 4 + 9 + 6 + 3 + 1 + 1 = 24. (40 is the total number of pets, not learners.)

items.q: How many learners have no pets?
items.e: No pets is the value 0. There are 4 dots above 0.

items.q: Which sentence best describes the shape of the data?
c: Most learners have 4 or more pets
The dots are spread out evenly
items.e: 4 + 9 + 6 = 19 of the 24 learners have 0, 1 or 2 pets. Most of the dots are on the left, and only a few are on the right.

items.q: One value is far away from the rest of the data. Which value is it?
items.e: The dot at 6 is on its own, with a gap at 5. All the other dots are between 0 and 4.

items.q: Each dot is one swimmer. What is the mode of the data?
items.e: The tallest stack of dots is above 6, so the mode is 6 laps. (7 is how many swimmers swam 6 laps, and 12 is the highest value.)

items.q: How many swimmers swam more than 6 laps?
items.e: More than 6 means 7, 8 or 12 laps: 5 + 2 + 1 = 8 swimmers. Do not count the swimmers who swam exactly 6.

items.q: Which numbers of laps did nobody swim?
items.e: There are no dots above 9, 10 and 11. This is a gap in the data. 3 and 12 each have one dot.

items.q: Which sentence best describes the shape of the data?
c: The swimmers are spread out evenly
Every swimmer swam a different number of laps
items.e: 4 + 7 + 5 = 16 of the 22 swimmers swam 5, 6 or 7 laps. The dots are bunched in the middle, with one far away at 12.

items.q: What is the mode of this data?
items.e: The mode is the category chosen most often: the tallest column. That is Netball. The mode is the sport, not the number 9.

items.q: How many learners chose AFL?
items.e: The scale is labelled in 2s, with a grid line for every 1. The AFL column ends on the line between 6 and 8, so 7.

items.q: What kind of data is “favourite sport”?
items.e: The answers are names of sports, so the data is categorical. The sports have no natural order, so it is nominal.

items.q: What is the mode of the shirt sizes?
items.e: The tallest column is M, so the mode is size M. (12 is how many learners, and XL is the biggest size, not the most common one.)

items.q: Shirt size is ordinal categorical data. What does ordinal mean here?
c: The sizes have an order: S, M, L, XL
Each size has a different colour
items.e: Ordinal data is in categories that have a natural order. S is smaller than M, M is smaller than L, and so on.

items.q: Which of these is numerical data?
c: The number of pets at home
items.e: Numerical data is counted or measured, so the answers are numbers. Favourite fruit and eye colour are nominal. Shirt size is ordinal.

items.q: Which of these is ordinal categorical data?
items.e: Never, sometimes, often, always are categories with an order. Colours and pets have no order (nominal). Number of brothers and sisters is numerical.

items.q: What is the mode of the family sizes?
items.e: The tallest column is above 4, so the mode is 4 people. (10 is how many families, and 6 is the biggest family.)

items.q: Which sentence best describes the shape of the data?
c: There are the same number of each size
items.e: 6 + 10 + 5 = 21 of the 26 families have 3, 4 or 5 people. The columns are tallest in the middle and short at each end.

items.q: A new learner with 3 pets joins 5C. What is the mode now?
items.e: Add one dot above 3: now 4 learners have 3 pets. The tallest stack is still above 1 (9 dots), so the mode is still 1 pet.

items.q: Thabo says, “Twice as many learners chose AFL as chose swimming.” Is he right?
c: Yes. AFL is the most popular sport.
No. Twice 10 is 20, but AFL got 25.
Yes. AFL got 25 and swimming got 10.
No. AFL got 5 and swimming got 2.
items.e: Swimming 10, AFL 25. Twice 10 is 20, and 25 is more than 20, so he is not right. (5 and 2 are grid spaces, not learners.)

items.q: How many learners come to school by car?
items.e: Each circle stands for 10 learners. The Car row has 8 circles: 8 × 10 = 80. (8 reads each circle as 1 learner.)

items.q: How many more learners come by car than walk?
items.e: Car: 8 circles = 80. Walk: 4 circles and half a circle = 40 + 5 = 45. 80 − 45 = 35. (Leaving out the half circle gives 80 − 40 = 40.)

items.q: How many learners walk, ride a bike or ride a scooter?
items.e: Walk 45, Bike 20, Scooter 15 (1 circle and half a circle). 45 + 20 + 15 = 80. (Leaving out the half circles gives 40 + 20 + 10 = 70. 8 counts the circles.)

items.q: Next term, 20 learners who come by car will walk instead. What should the Walk row show then?
items.e: Walk now: 45. 45 + 20 = 65 learners. 65 = 60 + 5: 6 circles for 60 and half a circle for 5.

items.q: Which conclusion is supported by the pictograph?
c: More learners come by car than walk and ride a scooter together.
The bus is the least common way to travel.
No learners come to school by train.
items.e: Car 80. Walk and scooter: 45 + 15 = 60. 80 is more, so this is supported. Walking (45) is not most of the 195 learners. Train was not in the survey, so we cannot tell. Scooter (15) is the least common.

items.q: How many learners read at least 3 books?
items.e: At least 3 means 3, 4 or 5 books: 6 + 3 + 1 = 10 learners. (4 leaves out the learners who read exactly 3. 21 is the learners who read 3 or fewer.)

items.q: How many books did these learners read altogether?
items.e: Multiply each number of books by its frequency: 0 × 2 + 1 × 5 + 2 × 8 + 3 × 6 + 4 × 3 + 5 × 1 = 0 + 5 + 16 + 18 + 12 + 5 = 56. (25 is the number of learners, and 15 adds 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5.)

items.q: Which conclusion is supported by the table?
c: 4D read more books than every other class.
Every learner in 4D read at least one book.
Most learners in 4D read 2 or 3 books.
Nobody read 6 books because the books were too long.
items.e: 2 or 3 books: 8 + 6 = 14 of the 25 learners, which is more than half. 2 learners read 0 books. The table has no data about other classes, and it does not tell us why.

items.q: The teacher says, “More than half the class read 2 or more books.” Is she right?
c: No. 7 learners read fewer than 2 books.
items.e: 2 or more books: 8 + 6 + 3 + 1 = 18 learners. Half of 25 is 12 and a half, and 18 is more, so she is right.

items.q: Which statement is supported by the graph?
c: It is 31 °C at 2 pm every day
It was warmer at 4 pm than at 10 am
items.e: 4 pm: 28 °C. 10 am: 27 °C. So 4 pm was warmer. The graph shows one day only, so it cannot tell us about every day. It does not show rain. 6 pm (26 °C) was warmer than 6 am (21 °C).

items.q: Which statement is supported by the graph?
c: It will rain again next Thursday
The tank was empty on Wednesday
The family used 500 ℓ every day
There was more water on Thursday than on Monday
items.e: Thursday: 4 500 ℓ. Monday: 4 000 ℓ. The water did not fall by 500 ℓ every day (Thursday to Friday it fell 250 ℓ). The graph cannot tell us about next week. On Wednesday there were still 3 000 ℓ.

items.q: After Sunday the family keeps using 500 ℓ each day, and it does not rain. How much water will be in the tank on Tuesday?
The tank can hold 5 000 ℓ. How much more water could it hold on Thursday?
items.e: On Thursday it held 4 500 ℓ. 5 000 − 4 500 = 500 ℓ more would fill it.

items.q: Ethan says, “My sunflower grew more than Ofentse’s, because it is taller in week 6.” Is he right?
items.e: Ofentse: 110 − 10 = 100 cm. Ethan: 115 − 15 = 100 cm. They grew the same amount. Ethan’s started taller, so it finished taller. (115 cm and 110 cm are heights, not growth.)

items.q: Which statement is supported by the dot plot?
c: Half the class has no pets
More learners have 1 pet than any other number
Learners with more pets are happier
items.e: 1 pet has the tallest stack (9 dots). Only 4 of the 24 learners have no pets, which is not half. The dot plot does not tell us how happy anyone is.

items.q: Which statement is supported by the graph?
c: There are 275 people at 2 pm every Saturday
It rained at 6 pm, so people went home
The beach was busiest at 2 pm
The beach was busiest at 6 pm
items.e: The highest point is at 2 pm (275 people). The graph does not show the weather, and it is one Saturday only, so it cannot tell us about every Saturday.

items.q: The surf club wants 1 lifeguard on duty for every 50 people at the beach (or part of 50). How many lifeguards are needed at 2 pm?
items.e: At 2 pm there were 275 people. 5 lifeguards cover 5 × 50 = 250 people. 25 people are left over, so 1 more is needed: 6 lifeguards.

items.q: Pieter goes for a swim when the temperature is 30 °C or more. At which readings was it 30 °C or more?
items.e: 12 pm: 30 °C and 2 pm: 31 °C. 30 °C counts, because it says 30 °C or more. 4 pm (28 °C) and 10 am (27 °C) are below 30.

items.q: Tebogo’s puppy weighed 3 kg at 2 months. At what age did it first weigh more than 3 times as much?
items.e: 3 × 3 kg = 9 kg. At 4 months it was 8 kg, which is not more than 9 kg. At 5 months it was 10 kg, so 5 months.
